dmm-2016-power-01a.title: Compute
dmm-2016-power-01a.body: $3\cdot5=15\equiv1$, so $3^{-1}=5$ and $5^{-1}=3$; $6\cdot6=36\equiv1$, so $6^{-1}=6$. Powers of $3$ mod $7$: $3,2,6,4,5,1$, so $\operatorname{ord}(3)=6$. Powers of $5$: $5,4,6,2,3,1$, so $\operatorname{ord}(5)=6$. Powers of $6$: $6,1$, so $\operatorname{ord}(6)=2$.

dmm-2016-power-01b.title: Compute
dmm-2016-power-01b.body: Powers of $2$: $2,4,1$, so $\langle2\rangle=\{1,2,4\}$. Powers of $3$: $3,2,6,4,5,1$, so $\langle3\rangle=T$.

dmm-2016-power-02b.title: Division with remainder
dmm-2016-power-02b.body: Write $d=kn+r$ with $0\le r<n$. Then $e=g^d=(g^n)^k*g^r=g^r$. By minimality of $n$, $r$ cannot be a positive integer, so $r=0$ and $n\mid d$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2016-power-03a.title: Subgroup of size k
dmm-2016-power-03a.body: *Subgroup:* $g^i*g^j=g^{i+j}\in\langle g\rangle$, and the inverse of $g^i$ is $g^{-i}=g^{kt-i}$ for any $t$ with $kt\ge i$, which is a power of $g$ (indeed $g^{kt}=e$). *Size:* $g^x=g^y$ iff $g^{x-y}=e$ iff $k\mid x-y$. So the powers $g^0,g^1,\dots,g^{k-1}$ are pairwise distinct and every other power equals one of them: $|\langle g\rangle|=k$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2016-power-03b.title: Lagrange
dmm-2016-power-03b.body: By Theorem 1 applied to the subgroup $\langle g\rangle$, $k=|\langle g\rangle|$ divides $|G|$. Since $|G|$ is a multiple of $k=\operatorname{ord}(g)$, $g^{|G|}=(g^k)^{|G|/k}=e$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2016-power-03c.title: Prime order
dmm-2016-power-03c.body: Let $n=\operatorname{ord}(g^i)$. Then $g^{in}=(g^i)^n=e$, so $k\mid in$ by problem 2b. Since $k$ is prime and $1\le i<k$, $\gcd(i,k)=1$, hence $k\mid n$. Conversely $(g^i)^k=(g^k)^i=e$, so $n\mid k$. Thus $n=k$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2016-power-03d.title: Either equal or trivial intersection
dmm-2016-power-03d.body: Suppose $\langle g\rangle\cap\langle b\rangle\ne\{e\}$: then $g^i=b^j\ne e$ for some $i,j$ not divisible by $k$. As $k$ is prime there is $m$ with $im\equiv1\pmod k$. Then $g=g^{im}=(g^i)^m=(b^j)^m=b^{jm}\in\langle b\rangle$, so $\langle g\rangle\subseteq\langle b\rangle$. Both sets have exactly $k$ elements, so $\langle g\rangle=\langle b\rangle$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2016-power-04b.title: Powers of a conjugate
dmm-2016-power-04b.body: Let $r=f_h(g)=h*g*h^{-1}$. Telescoping the $h^{-1}*h$ factors, $r^t=h*g^t*h^{-1}$ for every $t\ge1$. Hence $r^t=e\iff h*g^t*h^{-1}=e\iff g^t=h^{-1}*h=e$ (multiply on the left by $h^{-1}$ and on the right by $h$). So $r^t=e$ exactly when $g^t=e$, i.e. when $k\mid t$ (problem 2b); therefore $\operatorname{ord}(r)=k$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2016-power-04c.title: Injective on a finite set
dmm-2016-power-04c.body: If $f_h(g_1)=f_h(g_2)$ then $h*g_1*h^{-1}=h*g_2*h^{-1}$; multiplying by $h^{-1}$ on the left and by $h$ on the right gives $g_1=g_2$. So $f_h$ is injective, and an injective map from a finite set to itself is bijective. (Directly, $f_{h^{-1}}$ is its inverse.) $\blacksquare$

dmm-2016-power-05a.title: Lagrange inside P
dmm-2016-power-05a.body: $P$ is a group of order $p^k$ and $\operatorname{ord}(g)=|\langle g\rangle|$ divides $|P|=p^k$ (problem 3b applied in $P$). A divisor of $p^k$ is a power of $p$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2016-power-05b.title: Sylow counting
dmm-2016-power-05b.body:
$56=7\cdot8$. By Sylow (i),(ii), $n_7\mid8$ and $n_7\equiv1\pmod7$, so $n_7\in\{1,8\}$. If $n_7=1$, the unique Sylow $7$-subgroup $P$ satisfies $f_h(P)=P$ for all $h$ by (iii), so $P$ is a normal subgroup of order $7$, contradicting simplicity. Hence $n_7=8$.

An element of order $7$ generates a subgroup of order $7$, which is a Sylow $7$-subgroup. Each Sylow $7$-subgroup has exactly $6$ elements of order $7$ (the non-identity elements), and different Sylow $7$-subgroups meet only in $e$ (problem 3d). So $G$ has $8\cdot6=48$ elements of order $7$.

**Answer: $8$ Sylow $7$-subgroups and $48$ elements of order $7$.**

dmm-2016-power-05c.title: Count elements of orders 13 and 5
dmm-2016-power-05c.body: $520=13\cdot5\cdot8$. Suppose $G$ is simple. For $p=13$: $n_{13}\mid40$ and $n_{13}\equiv1\pmod{13}$, so $n_{13}\in\{1,40\}$. If $n_{13}=1$ the unique Sylow $13$-subgroup is normal by (iii), contradicting simplicity; so $n_{13}=40$, giving $40\cdot12=480$ elements of order $13$. For $p=5$: $n_5\mid104$ and $n_5\equiv1\pmod5$, so $n_5\in\{1,26\}$, and as before $n_5=26$, giving $26\cdot4=104$ elements of order $5$. Elements of different orders are different, so $G$ would have at least $480+104=584>520$ elements: a contradiction. Hence $G$ is not simple. $\blacksquare$
